# The Architecture Moonshot {#sec-moonshot}

::: {.epigraph}

**Governing question:** *What ambitious system-and-chip design capability is Architecture 2.0 trying to create, and what would count as achieving it?*

**Core thesis:** *Architecture 2.0 seeks to expand a compact request into a full-stack architecture exploration spanning workloads, software, microarchitecture, and physical signoff.*

Architecture 2.0 asks whether learned models, coupled directly to physical engineering tools and closed-loop feedback, can let an architecture study reach further than a manual flow allows. Such a study could revisit more of a design's hardware–software interfaces, memory hierarchy, and execution schedule. The moonshot is a design system capable of carrying high-level system intent through to a verified, physically realizable chip. Human architects set the requirements and decide which hardware and software choices the system may revise.

Historical precedents from Mead–Conway very-large-scale integration (VLSI), reduced instruction set computing (RISC), and logic synthesis show that a new design abstraction becomes practical only when engineers can implement it dependably and evaluate its trade-offs or check its correctness. An AI-native design system seeks to extend that pattern to coordinated hardware–software exploration. The Lighthouse mobile extended-reality (XR) challenge makes that breadth concrete. Its compact product request leaves coupled choices about workloads, software, hardware, and physical implementation to be resolved (@fig-ch01-cover-map).

![**From a system goal to evaluated candidate designs.** A compact system request expands into explicit constraints and workload specifications, driving closed-loop experiments across learned models and engineering tools before returning measured evidence for human review.](images/ch01-cover-map.svg){#fig-ch01-cover-map width="100%" fig-alt="Chapter overview diagram in which a system goal leads to explicit requirements, coordinated design experiments, and evaluation of the design and the effort needed to develop it, followed by human review."}

The evaluation at the right of the map separates the quality of the resulting chip from the engineering effort needed to develop it. A verified, physically realizable design that meets the agreed requirements would establish an engineering milestone. The complete method faces a separate test. It must improve the architecture result within a matched budget, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or both, relative to a credible conventional alternative. Human architects separately judge whether the result and remaining risks justify commitment to silicon. The moonshot remains a research target rather than an established capability.

## From Architectural Choices to a Design System {#sec-case-for-ai-native-design}

Consider an architect tasked with accelerating a target workload under fixed power and chip-area constraints. Increasing on-chip memory capacity can reduce stall cycles, but consumes precious die area and leakage power. Reorganizing the computation might extract more throughput from existing hardware, but demands extensive software rewrites. The architect's challenge is to determine which combination of microarchitectural and software choices satisfies the constraints, and whether the gains justify the design cost.

Each choice changes the work required elsewhere. A larger cache may need a different banking arrangement to meet timing, while a smaller scratchpad may require the compiler to divide computation into finer tiles. Architects must coordinate the implementation, simulation, and verification of each candidate before deciding what to try next. Architecture 2.0 asks whether a design system can carry out more of this coordinated exploration while keeping the system requirements fixed.

Machine learning contributes predictive, generative, and optimization techniques to this work.[^fn-historical-ai-c01] Learned cost models can rank tensor-program schedules before running them on hardware [@ChenEtAl2018AutoTVM]; generative models can draft initial register-transfer-level code [@VerilogEval]. An AI-native design system connects these components to engineering tools in a loop that proposes, evaluates, and revises hardware and software together.

[^fn-historical-ai-c01]: **Historical AI in Architecture**: Learning has a history both in hardware mechanisms, such as perceptron branch predictors [@JimenezLin2001Perceptron], and in design tools, such as predictive models for design-space exploration [@IpekEtAl2006PredictiveDSE]. This chapter concerns the design process, where learned components can help propose and assess changes to the hardware and software under study.

Each proposed memory subsystem passes through several tools. Cycle-level simulators measure performance, and synthesis and layout tools check timing and area. Thermal models check heat dissipation against package and cooling limits, and functional checks test conformance to the specification. If a candidate delivers high throughput but misses timing, the design system uses the electronic design automation (EDA) reports to guide a revision, such as pipelining a critical path, or to reject the candidate. Each result therefore helps determine the next architectural experiment.

The surrounding design system supplies information that a learned model cannot obtain from its trained weights alone. These weights are numerical parameters learned during training. They capture patterns in training data; they do not identify the current workload trace, the selected manufacturing process, or which hardware revision produced a timing failure. Even a foundation model, a pretrained model that can be adapted across tasks [@BommasaniEtAl2021FoundationModels], remains one component. The design system maintains the live project state, runs the tools, and links each measurement to the hardware and software that produced it. It can use analytical models and conventional optimizers wherever they serve the engineering task better than learned approximations. In that division of labor the learned model is optional, while the experiment inputs, engineering tools, and saved evaluations persist across every run (@fig-foundation-system).

![**A model contributes to an experiment run by the surrounding design system.** Project requirements, versioned hardware–software state, and tool settings supply the context for each run; learned and conventional methods use the measured results to select subsequent experiments, keeping a foundation model's pretrained weights separate from the live state of the current study [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20].](images/fig-foundation-system){#fig-foundation-system width="90%" fig-alt="System diagram in which requirements, matching hardware and software versions, and tool settings provide inputs to learned or conventional methods and engineering tools. Results are saved with the candidate that produced them and can guide the next experiment. A foundation model is one optional component."}

Building or adapting that system requires judgment about both the hardware and the learned components. A generated memory controller must satisfy its behavioral specification. A learned cost predictor must be trained on suitable examples and assessed on independent ones to determine how well its predictions generalize [@HastieTibshiraniFriedman2009Elements]. The architect therefore needs to understand how to direct the design loop and how to construct its models, tool connections, and checks.

## Lessons from Earlier Shifts in Design Automation {#sec-historical-context}

Architecture 2.0 would not be the first change in how architects design. Earlier transitions in computer architecture each gave designers a new way to express their intent, and each became practical only once engineers could trust what that new description produced. They show why a new automated workflow needs evidence that engineers can use to judge its results.

The Mead–Conway VLSI revolution decoupled topological circuit layout from foundry-specific fabrication recipes through scalable, dimensionless $\lambda$-rules [@MeadConway1980VLSI].[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01] Designers could compose complex layouts using a uniform geometric contract without managing individual process physics. This division of responsibility proved essential as transistor budgets expanded, because architects could focus on modular system composition while design rules supplied a checkable connection to the fabrication process.

[^fn-vlsi-complexity-c01]: **VLSI complexity (origin)**: Early-1980s frontier microprocessors held about $10^4$ to $10^5$ transistors, and by 2021 frontier chips held tens of billions [@Rupp2022MicroprocessorTrendData]. Mead and Conway answered that outgrowth of transistor-level practice with higher-level abstractions, design rules, and fabrication access that a course could teach and a community could share.

While Mead–Conway separated layout geometry from process physics, RISC showed that an instruction set architecture cannot be judged apart from compiler behavior and physical cycle time [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. An instruction's value depends on whether optimizing compilers actually use it and how much pipeline complexity it adds to the hardware. That insight made the compiler a full partner in architectural design. Architects began to judge an instruction set by end-to-end program runtime and clock rate rather than by the compactness of hand-written assembly code.

On the hardware implementation side, logic synthesis raised the level at which engineers describe circuits. Once architects specified computation as register-transfer level (RTL) operations on data and state, synthesis tools could translate those descriptions directly into optimized gate netlists [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization]. Synthesis earned engineering trust, however, only because it was paired with two verification pillars that made its output auditable: formal equivalence checking proved functional agreement between RTL and gates [@Formality], while static timing analysis (STA) checked path delays against declared clock and timing constraints without requiring exhaustive dynamic simulation.[^fn-formal-sta-c01] Generating a gate-level circuit and proving its functional and timing validity became inseparable halves of the design flow.

[^fn-formal-sta-c01]: **Equivalence checking and timing analysis**: Formal equivalence checking proves that two circuit representations (such as RTL source and a synthesized gate netlist) agree under the proof's state and input assumptions without enumerating simulation test vectors. STA checks setup and hold constraints using path delays and declared clock relationships at specified operating corners. Asynchronous clock-domain crossings require separate checks for synchronization and protocol safety.

Parameterized hardware generators extended this foundation by encoding entire families of microarchitectures as software programs. Hardware construction languages such as Chisel parameterize datapath bitwidths, cache capacities, and buffer depths, allowing generators to emit customized RTL descriptions across broad design spaces [@BachrachEtAl2012Chisel].[^fn-generators-c01] Yet parameterization alone does not resolve the design problem, because architects must still evaluate the generated instances. A generator is also bounded by its own family. It can encode alternative topologies or pipeline structures, but its existing parameters cannot express a repair outside the family it was written to construct.

[^fn-generators-c01]: **Hardware generators**: Unlike static register-transfer descriptions, hardware generators are programs written in host languages (such as Scala in Chisel) that emit a register-transfer description during an elaboration phase (Chisel produces an intermediate representation, FIRRTL, that is lowered to Verilog). Their parameters can select both dimensions and structural alternatives. Exploring beyond those alternatives requires revising the generator or supplying a different construction method.

As @fig-design-method-progression traces across these four transitions, new abstractions made larger design problems tractable when paired with dependable implementation and evaluation, from quantitative performance comparisons to automated verification checks.

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size diagram needs flexible float placement to stay near its historical discussion. -->
![**New design abstractions depend on implementation and evaluation.** Four established transitions connect higher-level design descriptions to implementation methods and to quantitative evaluation or correctness checks; the separately boxed Architecture 2.0 loop extends that pattern to coordinated hardware–software exploration as an active research target.](images/fig-design-method-progression){#fig-design-method-progression width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram in which four historical examples arranged in two rows connect VLSI design rules, instruction-set choices, RTL, and parameterized generators to implementations and their checks. A separate proposed system connects a system goal and current design files to methods, tools, and evaluated alternatives."}

Across these earlier shifts, the design process operated as *Architecture 1.0*, a methodology built around human architects in which languages, simulators, generators, and verification flows helped people explore alternatives and coordinate decisions across layers. *Architecture 2.0* asks what changes when automated search participates in making and revising those architectural decisions. Its proposed abstraction is a high-level system specification from which a design loop coordinates candidate generation, simulation, and physical implementation. How much of that coordination a system can perform depends on which design decisions it is permitted to revisit.

## Three Scopes of AI-Assisted Architecture {#sec-three-operational-layers}

When an engineering team treats all "AI for chip design" as one thing, expectations quickly outrun what a given tool can actually change. A local Verilog autocomplete model cannot relieve a system-wide memory bottleneck, and a parameter tuner cannot close a power gap if the frozen bus interface itself prevents every legal configuration from meeting the budget. The tasks themselves differ in how much coordination they need across the system stack. Drafting an isolated cache controller needs little, sweeping its capacities inside a fixed bus protocol needs more, and redesigning the memory hierarchy alongside its compiler runtime needs the most.

That coordination matters because computer architecture spans both the hardware–software contract and the physical structures that implement it: instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory hierarchy, interconnect fabrics, specialized accelerators, chiplet topologies, compiler schedules, and runtime interfaces. These parts of the stack depend on one another, so changing one in isolation often exposes a bottleneck in another. A wider vector datapath, for example, helps only if compiler vectorization, memory bandwidth, and thermal limits can feed and cool it.

To distinguish how much of this stack a workflow can adjust, Architecture 2.0 defines three operational layers [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. Rather than categorizing tools by the algorithms they run, the layers classify a workflow by which design decisions it may revisit. Architects still set the constraints, weigh cross-layer trade-offs, and make the final signoff decisions. Between those checkpoints, an AI-native system can run more of the search in a closed loop, which matters most when fixing a bottleneck requires changing hardware and software together.

Suppose a team must choose a memory subsystem for continuous sensor traffic under fixed performance, area, and power targets. The limiting factor may be bandwidth, area, or power, but the changes an automated workflow can explore depend on which parts of the design the human team has frozen. The three operational layers in @tbl-operational-layers-input-output differ in those permitted changes, the inputs they require, and the outputs they return. From Layer 1 to Layer 3, the team opens more of the hardware and software structure to search (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration).

- **Layer 1 (point assistance): Assistance with Individual Tasks within a Frozen Context.** A model performs an isolated task inside an existing architecture whose system organization, microarchitecture, interfaces, and tool flow remain fixed. In our memory study, a code-generation model might draft a first-in, first-out (FIFO) queue using the AXI4-Stream transfer protocol for the existing system-on-chip (SoC) interconnect. The engineer reviews the generated Verilog, fixes errors, connects the ports, and runs lint and timing checks. The model supplies a candidate artifact, while the engineer handles integration and decides what to run next.
- **Layer 2 (container-bound optimization): Parameter Optimization within an Immutable Formulation.** Given a target workload and power, performance, and area (PPA) constraints, an optimizer searches a parameterized architectural design space $\Theta$. Human architects fix the template, legal parameter ranges, and external interfaces before search begins, even when parameters select among different internal topologies. The optimizer varies the parameter vector $\theta \in \Theta$ in a closed loop with simulators or EDA tools. It returns the best configuration found, $\theta^*$, or an estimated Pareto frontier, a set of candidates for which improving one metric requires sacrificing another [@Deb2001MultiObjective]. In our memory study, it searches cache line sizes, capacities, and set associativities against cycle-accurate simulation while holding the processor–cache bus interface, coherence protocol, and workload binary fixed. If DRAM bandwidth remains the limiting factor after parameter tuning, the optimizer cannot change the memory interface or rewrite the software to escape it. Learned macro placement, which searches $(x,y)$ coordinates for circuit blocks within a fixed netlist, follows this same pattern [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement].
- **Layer 3 (AI-native design system): Specification-Driven Co-Design across Abstraction Boundaries.** The architect supplies workload requirements, physical PPA targets and process limits, and a correctness and verification contract, while permitting coordinated hardware–software changes beyond a single microarchitectural template. In our memory study, a prospective Layer 3 system could test whether replacing hardware-managed caching reduces area and power for streaming accesses. One candidate would combine an explicit scratchpad, software-managed direct memory access (DMA) descriptor queues, double-buffered streaming FIFOs, and matching compiler loop schedules that overlap compute with data transfers.[^fn-double-buffering-dma-c01] Physical tool feedback would guide revisions to the combined design before timing and power signoff. The workflow returns co-adapted candidates, measured metrics, and unmet constraints for human review; a run may reject its candidates or halt with unresolved violations.

[^fn-double-buffering-dma-c01]: **Double-buffering and descriptor chaining**: Double-buffering alternates between two memory banks so that a transfer into one bank overlaps computation on the other. A DMA controller moves data without requiring the processor to issue each transfer. Descriptor chaining lets it follow a sequence of transfer descriptions in memory, moving multiple data blocks without a processor interrupt for each block.

| **Operational layer** | **Inputs supplied to system** | **Fixed constraints (immutable contract)** | **Degrees of freedom (search space)** | **System output** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Layer 1: point assistance** | Human task query within existing design context | Complete system architecture, microarchitecture, interfaces, and tool flow | Localized syntax, logic, or scalar estimate for requested task | Isolated candidate artifact (code snippet, testbench, diagnostic report) |
| **Layer 2: container-bound optimization** | Workload, PPA targets, and parameterized architectural template $\Theta$ | Prescribed template, permitted parameter choices, and external interfaces | Parameter vector $\theta \in \Theta$ (e.g., capacities, unroll factors, macro coordinates) | Best configuration found, $\theta^* \in \Theta$, within prescribed parameterization |
| **Layer 3: AI-native design system** | Workload intent, physical PPA constraints, and verification contract | External workload requirements, physical budget, and correctness contract | Coordinated hardware–software changes: microarchitecture, arithmetic representation, dataflow, and software mapping | Co-adapted candidates, evaluation results, and unresolved constraints |
: **Operational layers differ in their input contracts and architectural degrees of freedom.** Each layer states what the human architect holds fixed, which decisions the automated system may reconsider, and what result it returns. {#tbl-operational-layers-input-output tbl-colwidths="[18,22,22,20,18]"}

![**Operational layers differ in what the design system may change.** Decisions struck through in the team's specification move from human-frozen assumptions into the automated search space: (a) Layer 1 drafts one block inside a frozen design for an engineer to integrate and check, (b) Layer 2 searches the parameters of a prescribed template $\Theta$ in a closed loop, and (c) Layer 3 opens the template itself, revising hardware and software together under physical evaluation.](images/fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration){#fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration width="100%" fig-alt="Diagram in which three stacked rows show the operational layers, with Layer 1 at the bottom and Layer 3 at the top. Each row lists what the team specifies, what the system works on, and the feedback it receives, and decisions the team no longer fixes appear struck through. Point assistance drafts one block inside a frozen pipeline for an engineer to integrate, container-bound optimization searches cache capacity, buffer depth, and macro placement within a fixed template, and an AI-native design system revises the compiler schedule, instruction extensions, arithmetic format, and buffering together under physical evaluation."}

The struck-through items in @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration mark design choices released from the team's fixed specification into the search space. Releasing a bus interface or memory organization allows the system to reconsider that choice alongside the software schedule; it does not release the workload requirements, physical budget, or correctness contract that every candidate must satisfy.

Scope also does not determine how rigorously a workflow evaluates its candidates (@fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration), because scope and evaluation fidelity answer different questions. A Layer 1 assistant can inspect a post-route timing report while the engineer decides what to edit next, and a Layer 2 optimizer can run full physical implementation inside a fixed template. Conversely, a Layer 3 workflow that may revise hardware and software interfaces together has not thereby shown an AI-native capability. Every candidate still has to pass the functional, timing, and physical checks that its intended use demands.

Just as the three layers are independent of evaluation fidelity, they are also distinct from the method families used inside each step. Prediction, generation, and optimization work across all three layers: a predictor estimates performance or physical cost, a generator drafts concrete artifacts (such as RTL modules, configurations, or compiler schedules), and an optimizer searches parameter or decision spaces to improve an objective. An agent is a software component that uses these methods, reads tool feedback, and chooses successive actions in a closed loop without a human between steps. The operational layers specify *which design decisions the workflow may revisit*, whereas method families specify *how each step is carried out* (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). The layers are also not a ranking. Each fits a different class of problem, and a well-scoped parameter search is often better served by a Layer 2 optimizer than by an open-ended Layer 3 system.[^fn-level2-vs-level3-c01]

[^fn-level2-vs-level3-c01]: **Layer 2 parameter sweeps versus Layer 3 structural adaptation**: Layer 2 workflows explore parameters $\theta \in \Theta$ within a prescribed architectural template. Changing pipeline depth remains Layer 2 when that choice is already encoded in the generator. Layer 3 permits coordinated revisions beyond the template, such as replacing a cache interface with software-managed transfers and adapting the compiler schedule to match. The distinction concerns the permitted formulation, not whether two generated netlists have identical graphs.

The wider scope of Layer 3 also creates room to explore organizations that depart from familiar human designs. A model trained on existing RTL can reproduce useful engineering conventions, but it also inherits historical choices about symmetry, buffer capacities, and module boundaries. An asymmetric memory hierarchy or an unusual pipeline may be worth testing even when it looks unfamiliar. The distinction is between conventions that help people manage a design and requirements that make the chip work. Functional correctness, safe communication between clock domains, manufacturing test access, and physical implementation limits remain binding even when the organization changes.

Game-playing systems offer a documented precedent for judging candidates by checks rather than by resemblance. AlphaGo Zero, trained only by self-play against the rules of Go, surpassed every earlier version that had been initialized from human expert games (@fig-demonstration-ceiling) [@SilverEtAl2017AlphaGoZero].

![**Strength followed checks against the rules of the game, not resemblance to human play.** Tournament Elo ratings of five AlphaGo versions evaluated at 5\ s per move [@SilverEtAl2017AlphaGoZero]. Hatched bars denote versions initialized from human expert games; self-play reinforcement learning against exact game outcomes drove ratings from 3,055 for the raw network to 5,185 for AlphaGo Zero.](images/fig-demonstration-ceiling){#fig-demonstration-ceiling width="95%" fig-alt="Horizontal bar chart of Elo ratings for five AlphaGo versions. AlphaGo Zero rates highest at 5,185, followed by AlphaGo Master at 4,858, AlphaGo Lee at 3,739, AlphaGo Fan at 3,144, and the AlphaGo Zero network without search at 3,055. Hatched bars mark the three versions that started from human expert games."}

Hardware has no equally cheap and exact referee. The rules of Go score a finished game exactly and at negligible cost, whereas a candidate microarchitecture needs simulation, implementation, and verification runs that take hours and can disagree. The lesson still transfers. A design system should select candidates by the physical and functional checks they pass, not by how closely they resemble existing RTL.

Testing that ambition needs a system problem large enough to expose the interactions among hardware and software choices. A wearable processor, whose software must meet frame deadlines without exceeding power and thermal limits, provides such a challenge.

## The Lighthouse Mobile XR Challenge {#sec-intent-vs-spec}

The *Lighthouse* project is this book's running design challenge. Its task is to design a mobile XR compute subsystem that runs concurrent perception and rendering workloads within the power, thermal, and latency budgets of a wearable device. An efficient arithmetic block alone cannot meet that goal if it waits on off-chip memory, stalls behind software dependencies, or exceeds the package's heat limits. Lighthouse keeps those full-system interactions in view. The complete design remains a research target rather than a completed silicon tapeout.

### A Compact Request and Coupled Choices

```{=latex}
\Needspace{7\baselineskip}
```

> **The Lighthouse goal.** Demonstrate by 2030 that an AI-native design system can expand a compact system request into candidate implementations spanning software, microarchitecture, and physical layout; quantify their PPA trade-offs; and deliver an implementation that satisfies system requirements and passes physical signoff.

Mobile XR makes those cross-layer trade-offs immediate. A frame delivered past its deadline breaks user immersion even when average throughput is high, and a brief burst of speed is useless if it drives the headset past its thermal limit. Benchmarks such as XRBench [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench] and end-to-end pipelines such as ILLIXR [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR] show why isolated microarchitectural tweaks rarely suffice. The benefit of reduced memory traffic depends partly on how the compiler schedules each frame, while peak compute throughput must be balanced against skin-temperature limits. We can state the Lighthouse challenge as the compact request a design team might hand an automated system:

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

::: {.callout-lighthouse}
Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for an XRBench-class real-time mobile XR workload. The implementation may use a vector-capable central processing unit (CPU), an accelerator, or a system-on-chip (SoC) block. It must target a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope in a 3\ nm-class low-power mobile process.

Return a design-space report that explains which candidates were tested, how they compared, and which design the team should investigate further.
:::

The Lighthouse prompt is intentionally brief. It names a workload class and top-level physical targets, but leaves decisions open across eight coupled requirement domains: workload, instruction and application interfaces, compute organization, memory and data movement, power and thermal limits, compiler and runtime, physical constraints, and verification (@fig-moonshot-prompt).

<!-- arch2-allow: figure-placement-override The print-size diagram needs flexible float placement to stay near the Lighthouse prompt. -->
![**A compact request leaves many architectural decisions open.** Translating the two-paragraph Lighthouse prompt into a testable chip requires resolving interdependent choices across workloads, instruction interfaces, compute engines, memory hierarchy, thermal packaging, runtime scheduling, process libraries, and verification contracts.](images/fig-moonshot-prompt){#fig-moonshot-prompt width="100%" fig-pos="!htbp" fig-alt="Diagram in which the Lighthouse prompt expands into workload, ISA and ABI, compute, memory, power, software, process, and verification decisions, which feed design experiments and engineering review."}

The connections among these domains determine whether a promising local choice helps the whole device. A design tuned for visual-inertial odometry alone may stall when neural rendering and depth reconstruction contend for the same memory bandwidth. The team therefore needs specific kernels, inputs, and execution traces rather than a workload name alone [@KwonEtAl2023XRBench]. Those traces must also preserve software dependencies. Perception, pose estimation, and rendering can be pipelined across frames, so the display's frame interval differs from each stage's deadline and from end-to-end motion-to-photon latency [@HuzaifaEtAl2021ILLIXR].

The compute organization must serve that software. The team might divide work among vector cores, neural processing units (NPUs), and fixed-function engines. An NPU built as a systolic array streams data across a regular grid of processing elements,[^fn-systolic-array-c01] so its efficiency depends on whether the compiler can tile tensors to keep the array supplied. A vector core brings its own instruction-set and software consequences. Adding the RISC-V vector extension changes the instructions software can use [@RISCV2026UnprivilegedISA] and enlarges the state an operating system may need to save on a context switch [@RISCV2026PrivilegedISA]. The application binary interface (ABI), which governs register conventions and parameter passing, must also match the chosen software stack.[^fn-abi-c01]

Memory choices connect these software decisions to area and power. A baseline might combine private caches, a shared last-level cache, and tightly coupled memory (TCM) scratchpads.[^fn-tcm-scratchpad-c01] Larger caches can cut off-chip DRAM traffic but consume die area and leakage power. A scratchpad gives software more control over data movement, but its benefit depends on the tile schedule and transfer overhead. Neither choice can be judged from the memory block alone. The 3\ W accounting boundary must include the affected data movement, and a thermal model must establish whether the package can dissipate the heat for the required duration. The same power is harder to dissipate in a passively cooled eyeglass temple than in a tethered pack or actively cooled headset.[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]

Physical implementation makes the remaining assumptions concrete. Calling a process "3\ nm-class" names a technology generation; synthesis and place-and-route tools need a particular process design kit (PDK),[^fn-pdk-c01] characterized standard cell libraries,[^fn-liberty-corners-c01] memory implementations, and metal layer stack. These determine which circuits can be built and how they behave across process, voltage, and temperature conditions. Functional behavior, bus protocol compliance, clock-domain crossings, and power-state transitions then require checks appropriate to the selected implementation.

[^fn-abi-c01]: **Application binary interface (ABI)**: While an ISA specifies machine instruction semantics, the ABI governs runtime conventions including caller- versus callee-saved register allocation, parameter passing, and stack alignment. These conventions set how much register state a function call must preserve. Operating system context switches are a separate cost, governed by how much architectural state the ISA defines (for example, the vector register file) and by whether the kernel saves it eagerly or lazily.

[^fn-systolic-array-c01]: **Systolic arrays**: A spatial grid of processing elements that pass data directly to neighboring elements on successive clock cycles. This organization reuses weights and activations while reducing repeated accesses to a central register file. Arithmetic units can sit idle when tensor dimensions do not tile evenly across the grid or memory bandwidth cannot supply its boundaries.

[^fn-tcm-scratchpad-c01]: **Tightly coupled memory (TCM)**: An on-chip static random-access memory (SRAM) block mapped directly into the physical memory address space, providing predictable access latency under its declared arbitration and access conditions. Unlike hardware-managed caches, scratchpads rely on software or DMA to schedule data transfers, eliminating tag-check energy overhead and nondeterministic cache-miss latency in real-time deadlines.

[^fn-xr-glasses-thermal-c01]: **Mobile XR and Smart Glasses Thermal Boundaries**: A power target alone does not determine the temperature of a wearable surface. Heat paths through the package and frame, ambient conditions, and duration of operation affect the temperature where the device contacts skin, and product-safety standards limit that temperature for prolonged contact. The study must select an enclosure, define its allowed surface temperature and contact conditions, and establish whether it can sustain the power target. A tethered compute unit or actively cooled head-mounted display changes the heat paths and therefore the feasible operating envelope.

These checks have direct architectural consequences. When an accelerator connects to an Arm Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) crossbar, its controller must obey handshake rules even when downstream memory stalls [@Arm2020AXI]. Backpressure occurs when the receiver deasserts `READY` while `VALID` remains asserted, requiring the sender to hold its data stable.[^fn-axi-backpressure-c01] A controller that mishandles backpressure may look fast in an isolated testbench that never stalls, yet lock up the system bus under real memory traffic. The memory organization, software schedule, and communication protocol have to work together.

[^fn-axi-backpressure-c01]: **AXI protocol handshakes**: On-chip AXI interconnects govern data transfers through paired `VALID` (producer) and `READY` (consumer) control signals across independent address, data, and response channels.

[^fn-pdk-c01]: **Process design kit (PDK)**: The package for one manufacturing process that supplies device models, design rules, and related data used by implementation tools. The open SKY130 PDK demonstrates that a PDK can be published [@SkyWater2020SKY130PDK], but it cannot supply the authorized project-specific information for a different process or commercial tool flow.

[^fn-liberty-corners-c01]: **Characterized cell libraries**: Tabulated databases (typically in Liberty `.lib` format) generated from low-level Simulation Program with Integrated Circuit Emphasis (SPICE) simulations that record the propagation delay, transition time, and leakage power of standard logic cells across discrete process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) operating corners.

### A Focused Memory-and-Tiling Study

The coupled domains define the breadth of the challenge, but a useful study need not search all of them at once. Suppose the Lighthouse team asks whether co-designing the memory hierarchy and software tiling can meet frame deadlines within the 3\ W envelope. Tiling divides a computation into smaller blocks so that their data can remain in on-chip memory while the processor or accelerator uses them. Smaller tiles may fit a smaller buffer, but they can also require more transfers and synchronization. This gives the team a concrete reason to vary hardware and software together.

The high-level request becomes an executable specification when the team states what stays fixed, what may change, and what the tools must check. For this study, the workload definitions, input data, externally imposed arrival and dependency requirements, ISA, application interfaces, process libraries, package assumptions, and product requirements stay fixed. The system may go beyond the existing cache-based template by replacing its hardware-managed cache interface with a software-managed scratchpad and DMA transfers, revising the transfer protocol and compiler schedule together. It can then tune memory capacities, scratchpad banking, tile dimensions, and DMA descriptor queues within each proposed organization. The system regenerates or recaptures candidate-dependent execution and memory traces as schedules and data transfers change. Fixing the surrounding assumptions keeps the experiment focused without requiring the whole system organization to be settled in advance.

The checks follow from those choices. Cycle-level simulation measures frame latency and memory stalls. Reference outputs and declared numerical tolerances test whether the tiled computation preserves the required behavior, including any changes in floating-point operation order. Synthesis and physical implementation test timing and area, while power and thermal models account for the affected on-chip blocks and off-chip transfers over the required operating duration. Shrinking a buffer cannot count as a power improvement if the study simply omits the additional DRAM traffic it causes.

We can then compare the joint search with credible conventional approaches that tune memory alone, tune software alone, or coordinate both without learned components. Comparing their feasible candidates on a Pareto frontier may reveal a useful new organization, but it may also show that a simpler cache change suffices or leave the target unresolved. Exhausting a search budget does not prove that no feasible design exists. This remains a prospective study; the book does not claim that the Lighthouse subsystem has been implemented or has met its targets.

When the team defines this study, language models can help draft the specification by extracting constraints from product documents or identifying ambiguous deadlines. Human architects still decide what problem the study should solve. The practical life cycle in @sec-architecture-20-ontology develops how that agreed specification becomes a sequence of proposals, tool runs, and revisions. Here, the example shows how far the moonshot reaches and how much work separates a compact request from a design problem that engineering tools can test.

## Assessing Progress Toward the Moonshot {#sec-efficiency-claims-need-rejectable-loops}

A completed Lighthouse design would be a substantial engineering achievement, but it would not by itself show that the design method improved architecture work. An expensive demonstration can establish technical feasibility without reducing development cost, and a sound method can remain useful even if market conditions prevent a tapeout. Progress therefore has three distinct meanings:

1. **The engineering milestone:** Can an AI-native design system translate a compact request into a verified, physically realizable design that satisfies the agreed requirements and passes signoff by 2030? This tests end-to-end capability within declared workloads, tools, and constraints. Establishing that a specification cannot be met can provide valuable insight, but it does not complete this implementation milestone.
2. **The methodological value:** Does the complete design system improve the architecture result within a matched budget, reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable result, or both, relative to a credible conventional alternative? Matching a baseline establishes feasibility within the study; an improvement gives teams a reason to adopt the method within that assessed scope.
3. **The commitment decision:** Should the resulting design be manufactured? Human decision makers must weigh the technical result alongside market timing, manufacturing cost, and residual risk. A decision to tape out neither proves that the method was efficient nor follows automatically from a successful research demonstration.

### What the Candidate Has Demonstrated

The engineering milestone depends on what tools have established about the candidate. In the Lighthouse memory study, a larger cache might reduce simulated frame latency yet exceed the area budget during physical implementation. That result can guide the next experiment toward a different banking layout or finer software tiling. It does not establish a feasible chip.

To say what a result has established, we need to separate the candidate from the artifacts built from it. The candidate is the hardware–software configuration under test. RTL, gate netlists, floorplans, and software binaries are artifacts built from that configuration; the architectural conclusion depends on measurements and checks of those artifacts. Fast analytical models and learned surrogates, which predict expensive tool results from previously evaluated designs, can help choose which candidates deserve further work [@ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Their estimates cannot establish that a design will route successfully or meet timing. Cycle-level simulation tests execution behavior, while physical signoff requires the timing, layout, and power-delivery checks accepted for the target manufacturing process.[^fn-physical-signoff-c01]

[^fn-physical-signoff-c01]: **Physical signoff**: The checks required before releasing mask data for semiconductor fabrication, or tapeout. They include static timing closure across the required operating corners, layout-versus-schematic agreement, design rule checking of layout geometry against manufacturing limits, and power-grid voltage-drop analysis. The target foundry or fabrication service determines the accepted tools, models, and rule decks.

Each result supports a conclusion at the level it actually tested. A functional unit test can establish the tested block behavior without establishing safe communication across clock domains or system-wide progress under contention. The verification and feedback methods in @sec-feedback-verification-trust develop how such evidence guides revisions. For the moonshot, the essential distinction is that generating an artifact, finding a promising candidate, and demonstrating a physically realizable system are different achievements.

### The Cost of the Complete Method {#sec-data-scarcity-verification-load}

The methodological test compares both the design quality and the effort required to obtain it. Design quality includes workload performance, dynamic and leakage power, die area, and thermal margins. Engineering effort includes the human and machine work spent preparing the design system, exploring candidates, and checking the result. Model adaptation, tool integration, compiler changes, failed runs, license use, and manual debugging all contribute to that cost.

A faster candidate does not by itself establish a productivity gain. The Lighthouse team might spend more time repairing generated testbenches than it saves in proposing memory configurations. Conversely, a workflow that reaches a comparable design with less total effort can be valuable even when its final PPA matches the conventional result. Credible baselines must have the same task, tool access, and comparison budget, including strong conventional methods that already coordinate hardware and software.

Amdahl's law explains why speeding up one task cannot determine the gain for the entire project [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. If a fraction $f$ of the original work is accelerated by a factor $s$ and the rest is unchanged, the overall speedup is $S = 1/((1-f) + f/s)$. This assumes the original work allocation remains applicable and no new overhead appears. Faster RTL drafting may leave verification and physical implementation unchanged, or increase them when more candidates require checking. Teams must measure those effects and distinguish human effort from elapsed time, since parallel or unattended runs can change one without reducing the other.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Credit a design method only for a better result or a lower total cost"}
**The principle:** Judge a design method against a credible alternative given the same task, tool access, and budget. It earns credit only when it improves the architecture result, reduces the total effort of reaching a comparable result, or both.

**The application:** Count the effort spent preparing the design system as well as running it. A better candidate can establish a quality gain within a matched budget, but it does not by itself establish a reduction in engineering cost.
:::

### Published Steps Toward the Moonshot

Published work shows useful progress at narrower scopes. VerilogEval tests whether generated hardware descriptions pass functional unit testbenches [@VerilogEval; @PinckneyEtAl2024RevisitingVerilogEval]. This helps assess a model for local RTL drafting, but it does not measure the resulting architecture's efficiency or physical timing closure. Learned macro placement instead searches block coordinates within a fixed netlist [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement]. It demonstrates optimization inside a prescribed structure, with continuing debate over how gains in placement objectives carry through to routed PPA [@ChengEtAl2026UpdatedAssessment].

Industrial projects also combine learned techniques across a chip program. OpenAI's reports on its Jalapeño inference accelerator describe model-assisted logic optimization and generated software kernels, while physical implementation proceeded through a partnership with Broadcom [@OpenAI2026JalapenoFirstResults; @Smith2026JalapenoIEEE]. These reports illustrate how several bounded tools can contribute to a chip. They do not provide a controlled comparison of total engineering cost against a matched conventional baseline or establish a closed loop in which physical feedback revises microarchitectural interfaces and software together.

A useful component need not solve the full Lighthouse challenge. The larger claim remains open until a complete system demonstrates the permitted cross-layer revisions, meets the implementation requirements, and earns its place against credible alternatives. The complete-system comparisons in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect examine that methodological test in depth.

## Human Review and Design Decisions {#sec-from-architecture-10-to-architecture-20}

As automated search takes on more proposals and tool runs, architects must decide which choices belong inside that search. A Lighthouse system may be authorized to revise the memory organization and compiler schedule within a 3\ W budget. It has no authority to raise the power limit when its candidates fail. Relaxing a frame deadline or increasing voltage beyond the approved operating envelope requires human judgment about the requirements and their consequences.

Human review also concerns the reasoning behind a recommendation. If the system favors a scratchpad over a cache, the architect must judge whether the workload assumptions represent the intended product and whether the evidence justifies the trade-off. Domain specialists assess implementation and verification results, and an accountable human authority decides whether to commit the design to manufacturing. The fuller account of those responsibilities belongs to @sec-what-architect-owns.

## How the Rest of This Book Is Organized

The chapters ahead teach architects both to direct AI-native design systems and to build or adapt their components. The opening arc examines the pressures that make coordinated exploration difficult (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales), then gives a self-contained overview of the design life cycle (@sec-architecture-20-ontology). The technical chapters develop the data and representations that hold the design state (@sec-data-representations-world-models), prediction, generation, and optimization methods (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), execution through engineering tools (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces), and verification and feedback that guide revision and learning (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). The closing arc examines transfer across the stack (@sec-loop-patterns-across-stack), evaluation of the complete system, including adversarial tests of its objectives and measurements (@sec-evaluating-agentic-architect), human architectural judgment (@sec-what-architect-owns), and the shared infrastructure needed to develop the discipline (@sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem).

## Open Questions

Every chapter in this book closes with a short set of questions that its argument depends on but does not settle. The moonshot leaves questions about how much of the design problem a system can take on and what would make that broader search useful:

- **When a short prompt leaves out key system details, how can a design tool tell which missing requirements will actually change the hardware?** A brief request may say nothing about memory ordering, thermal time constants, or tail-latency limits. If the system fills in those blanks silently, it may optimize the wrong product; if it asks the human architect about every unspecified parameter, automation loses its value. The challenge is to identify which ambiguities could change the preferred organization before paying for a full implementation study.
- **How can we verify unconventional microarchitectures that step outside familiar human design templates?** Human architects rely on symmetric pipeline stages, power-of-two buffer capacities, and standard bus handshakes partly because those regular idioms keep mental models and formal verification tractable. An AI-native design system guided by physical tool feedback could propose asymmetric memory hierarchies or irregular datapath staging that perform better. The open problem is how to explore such organizations while preserving the functional, communication, and manufacturing-test properties that make them implementable.
- **When a chip fails timing or routing late in physical design, how do we trace that failure back to the microarchitectural or compiler choice that caused it?** Static timing analysis and place-and-route tools report physical symptoms, such as a path that misses its timing constraint or congestion around a memory macro. An effective revision may require repartitioning a scratchpad bank, changing a pipeline, or restructuring a compiler schedule. Synthesis, placement, and routing transform the design through many discrete choices, making it difficult to identify which upstream change will repair the failure.
- **When is it worth allowing a design system to change an existing architectural template or interface?** Such changes expand the candidate space and invalidate some checks of the original module boundaries. Architects need ways to judge whether the resulting design freedom justifies the additional search and verification work. The unresolved question is when that broader scope can uncover useful organizations that even a joint hardware–software search within the original template cannot reach.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{12\baselineskip}
```

## Summary

The Architecture 2.0 moonshot is a design system that can carry compact system intent into coordinated hardware–software exploration and a verified, physically realizable result. Lighthouse makes that ambition concrete through an XR compute subsystem within a 3\ W wearable envelope. Its memory-and-tiling study shows why a short request leaves substantial architectural work open, and how a focused experiment can preserve those system constraints while reconsidering the organization beneath them. The challenge remains prospective. The engineering milestone, the benefit of the complete design method, and the human decision to manufacture are separate judgments.

::: {.callout-takeaways}
- **Match the workflow layer to the problem.** Use point assistance (Layer 1) for individual tasks, container-bound optimization (Layer 2) for search within prescribed templates, and an AI-native design system (Layer 3) when the study calls for coordinated hardware–software revisions beyond those templates.
- **Distinguish a model from a design system.** Learned weights supply reusable patterns; the surrounding system maintains the current project state, runs tools, and uses feedback to revise candidates.
- **Turn compact intent into a scoped design problem.** The Lighthouse request opens coupled workload, software, hardware, and physical choices. A study must state what remains fixed, what may vary, and what constitutes success.
- **Judge the complete method by quality and effort.** A design system earns its place through a better architectural result within a matched budget, lower total cost for a comparable result, or both against credible conventional alternatives.
- **Separate demonstration from commitment.** A physically realizable design meets an engineering milestone. Human architects still decide whether its trade-offs and remaining risks justify manufacturing.
:::

Manual workflows struggle to realize this full-stack design ambition, and automated assistance helps only where it relieves a real constraint. Which constraints bind depends on the transistor scaling limits, workload shifts, and verification bottlenecks that now strain chip design (@sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales).
